label: Synthesis direction and the primer requirement

source_excerpts.text: DNA strands are anti-parallel, new strands are synthesized in the 5′ to 3′ direction and the complementary strands run in the opposite 3′ to 5′ direction.

DNA synthesis occurs only in the 5′ to 3′ direction, meaning new bases are being added to the 3′ end of an existing strand. DNA polymerase can only add new bases to the 3′ end of an existing complementary strand. It can't synthesize a complementary strand of DNA from scratch.

When DNA replication occurs, gaps form between the ends of newly synthesized segments. DNA ligase closes this gap in the sugar phosphate backbone without adding new bases to the 3′ of the growing strand.

Before this happens, primase synthesizes a short sequence of RNA that is complementary to the DNA on the top strand. The new result is RNA primer because it prepares (primes) the strand for DNA polymerase. Unlike DNA polymerase, primase can start synthesis from scratch on a single stranded template strand. Once the primer is made, DNA polymerase can start adding deoxyribonucleotides.

DNA polymerase can't synthesize a complementary strand of DNA from scratch and the enzyme can only work if the new complementary strand has already been started. The enzyme can add deoxyribonucleotides to the ribonucleotides that are hydrogen bonded to a complementary DNA strand.

intro_1.teaching_goal: DNA polymerase adds new pieces only to the 3′ end.

intro_2.teaching_goal: New DNA only grows from 5′ to 3′.

intro_3.teaching_goal: DNA polymerase can't start a new strand from nothing.

intro_4.teaching_goal: Primase makes a short RNA primer, and DNA polymerase builds onto it.

intro_5.teaching_goal: New DNA grows 5′ to 3′, and it needs a primer to start.

direction_followup.teaching_goal: Explain growth direction and which end grows
key_points: Show each new nucleotide joining the 3′ end

direction_followup_2.teaching_goal: Explain growth direction and which end grows
direction_followup_2.approach: Start from the wrong idea: try to add a nucleotide at the 5′ end and show it can't join, then show it joining at the 3′ end.

primer_followup.teaching_goal: Explain why DNA polymerase needs a primer
key_points: Start from a bare template: polymerase can't begin
Primase lays down an RNA primer

primer_followup_2.teaching_goal: Explain why DNA polymerase needs a primer
primer_followup_2.approach: Put primase and DNA polymerase side by side on a bare template: primase can start from scratch, DNA polymerase can only extend what is already there.

review_points: New nucleotides join the 3′ end, so strands grow 5′→3′
DNA polymerase can't start a strand; primase makes an RNA primer it can extend
